On-screen pill: 'adults with HFpEF + obesity (BMI 30+) · vs placebo · ~2 years · NEJM 2024'. One line: HFpEF = a stiff heart that doesn't fill well. plan.why:
Spin-off of L1, to drive traffic to the long video. It uses the proven format of a named drug plus one number, with tirzepatide in the title. | fact-check: The SUMMIT one-number Short is a good fit and pairs with L1. Two changes are needed.
(1) The status line must say clearly that tirzepatide is NOT FDA-approved for heart failure as of Oct 2026. Lilly withdrew its HFpEF application in 2025. Saying only 'date any approval status' risks implying an indication.
(2) The working title says 'Heart Failure' in general. SUMMIT studied only HFpEF + obesity (BMI 30+), so the title must name that population.
Secondary sources give the composite figure as a 38% relative reduction (HR 0.62). The script must pair it with the absolute event rates per arm from the NEJM paper, as the craft rules require. Note that SUMMIT included adults with and without T2D.

package.title: Tirzepatide HFpEF: Worse HF or CV Death 9.9% vs 15.3% Placebo #shorts
package.description:
Can tirzepatide help one type of heart failure? In SUMMIT, adults with obesity and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) had cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure in 9.9% on tirzepatide vs 15.3% on placebo over about 2 years (HR 0.62) — mostly fewer worsening-HF events; cardiovascular deaths alone didn't differ significantly. Side effects, mainly gut-related, led more people to stop tirzepatide (6.3% vs 1.4% on placebo). Not FDA-approved for heart failure as of Oct 2026.

#GLP1 #Tirzepatide #HeartFailure #HFpEF

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. If you have heart failure, don't change your treatment without your care team. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
Packer M, et al. Tirzepatide for Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction and Obesity. N Engl J Med 2025;392:427-437. https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2410027
Lilly Withdraws Tirzepatide Application to FDA for Heart Failure. ConscienHealth, 2025. https://conscienhealth.org/2025/05/03/lilly-withdraws-tirzepatide-application-to-fda-for-heart-failure/

social.instagram_caption:
Tirzepatide (Zepbound) and one type of heart failure (HFpEF): what SUMMIT found. Not FDA-approved for heart failure as of Oct 2026.

In the SUMMIT trial, adults with obesity and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) — a stiff heart that doesn't fill well — took tirzepatide or placebo for about 2 years.

Cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure: 9.9% on tirzepatide vs 15.3% on placebo (HR 0.62).

The catch: the benefit was driven mostly by fewer worsening-HF events (8.0% vs 14.2%). Cardiovascular deaths alone didn't differ significantly.

Side effects led more people to stop tirzepatide: 6.3% vs 1.4% on placebo, mainly gut-related.

As of Oct 2026, tirzepatide isn't FDA-approved to treat heart failure — Lilly withdrew that application in 2025 after the FDA asked for another trial. It's approved for type 2 diabetes, weight management, and moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Save this if you or someone you love lives with HFpEF and obesity — it's worth bringing to your next appointment.

script.cta: The full SUMMIT breakdown is on our channel: "Does Tirzepatide (Zepbound) Help Heart Failure? What the SUMMIT Trial Found". If you have heart failure, don't change your treatment without your care team. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary: The core claims check out against the SUMMIT abstract (NEJM, online Nov 16 2024; 2025;392:427-437). The trial had 731 adults with an ejection fraction of 50% or more and a BMI of 30 or more. The composite of cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure was 9.9% vs 15.3% (HR 0.62). Worsening heart-failure events were 8.0% vs 14.2% (HR 0.54). Cardiovascular death was 2.2% vs 1.4% (HR 1.58, 95% CI 0.52–4.83), which wasn't significant. Median follow-up was 104 weeks, so "about two years" is fine. The approval status is right as of Oct 2026. FDA pages confirm Zepbound for chronic weight management (Nov 8 2023) and for moderate-to-severe OSA in adults with obesity (Dec 20 2024). Mounjaro was approved for type 2 diabetes on May 13 2022. Lilly withdrew its US application for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) in May 2025 after the FDA asked for a confirmatory trial. The script splits the composite result honestly into its parts, gives absolute rates with the HR, states the population, credits side effects to the right trial and includes the prescriber line. I found only minor wording and precision issues, with exact fixes below. I couldn't open the NEJM, PubMed or ConscienHealth pages myself (403 errors and a cookie wall). The SUMMIT figures were confirmed through an abstract excerpt in search results and the PMC Circulation companion paper. The ConscienHealth article exists, and search results confirm what it says.

issues.claim: In SUMMIT, gut symptoms were also the main side effects.
issues.problem: The SUMMIT abstract reports that adverse events leading to stopping the drug were mainly gastrointestinal (6.3% on tirzepatide vs 1.4% on placebo). The script's wording is broader than what the abstract says, and it gives no number.
issues.fix: In SUMMIT, side effects that led people to stop the drug were mainly gut-related: 6.3% on tirzepatide versus 1.4% on placebo.

issues.claim: approved as Zepbound ... for obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity
issues.problem: The FDA indication is moderate to severe OSA in adults with obesity. Leaving out the severity qualifier makes the scope sound wider than the label.
issues.fix: Narration: "...and as Zepbound for weight management and for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity." List item: "Moderate-severe sleep apnea with obesity (Zepbound): FDA-approved"

issues.claim: As of October 2026, tirzepatide isn't FDA-approved to treat heart failure.
issues.problem: The status is correct, but it leaves out why, and source S6 is cited without anything in the script drawing on it. Lilly withdrew its US heart failure application in 2025 after the FDA asked for another trial. Adding that reason stops the line sounding like a pending approval.
issues.fix: As of October 2026, tirzepatide isn't FDA-approved to treat heart failure; Lilly withdrew its US application in 2025 after FDA asked for another trial.

issues.claim: Zepbound's tirzepatide, in one type of heart failure.
issues.problem: The narration is a fragment, and it doesn't ask the plain question the hook pattern and on-screen text promise. 'Zepbound's tirzepatide' also puts the brand name first, which goes against the house style of generic name first.
issues.fix: Can tirzepatide, the medicine in Zepbound, help one type of heart failure?

issues.claim: More on our channel. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
issues.problem: The audience includes people already being treated for heart failure. A short safety line would stop anyone reading the result as a reason to change their current heart failure medicines.
issues.fix: More on our channel. If you have heart failure, don't change your treatment without your care team. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

notes: Caption card ends on a comma: 'CAN TIRZEPATIDE,' — banned caption ending.
Second caption card 'HELP ONE TYPE' is an awkward fragment that doesn't read as a complete phrase on its own.
Caption card ends on a comma: 'IN THE SUMMIT TRIAL,' — banned ending.
Caption spells out the number instead of using the numeral: 'VERSUS FIFTEEN POINT' instead of '15.3%'.
The number is split mid-value across caption cards ('FIFTEEN POINT' with the rest presumably on the next card), which the rules explicitly forbid.
Captions spell numbers out and fragment them nonsensically: 'THREE PERCENT ON PLACEBO.' then 'POINT SIX TWO.' — this garbles the actual figure and doesn't match any stat pill shown.
No stat/label title is on screen to anchor what number is being discussed, so the spoken number reads as disconnected noise.
Automated finding: speech bubble 'Feeling a bit stiff...' overlaps the caption 'HEART THAT DOESN'T' (t=31.48), both competing for the same lower-middle band.
Caption ends on 'DOESN'T', an incomplete auxiliary verb hanging mid-thought.
Captions spell the numbers out instead of matching the stat pill numerals: 'EIGHT PERCENT VERSUS' and 'FOURTEEN POINT TWO PERCENT.' instead of '8.0%' and '14.2%'.
This is the same repeat violation flagged in QA notes for 10-13 pieces.
Caption ends on 'DIDN'T', leaving the claim ambiguous for a beat ('cardiovascular deaths didn't' — didn't what?).
Empty placeholder cells with bare dashes ('–') are visible in the background grid, top and bottom of frame — these should never render with no content.
Automated finding: caption 'Stomach / diarrhoea and constipation,' overlaps the 'Stomach' tag at t=50.69.

audio.soundNotes: Music under voice (-13.5 dB) and in pauses (-14.5 dB) already sit in the target window, so gain stays at 1.0. Main fixes: thinned clustered transition cues that stacked 5–7 effects per second (e.g. ~30.4–31.5s, ~52s, ~85–87s) by dropping duplicate swoosh/whoosh layers fired at the same timestamp; pulled down two cues that read far louder than the voice during speech (blip at 46.77s was only -5.4 dB under voice, swoosh at 85.70s was -9.8 dB) to the -15/-17 dB felt range. Added four bespoke SFX to underline the heart-failure story beats (opening heartbeat pulse, a strained "stiff heart" creak, a deflating twist on the "not approved" reveal, and a warm resolving chime on the prescriber close) without adding to the stock-cue density.
